blocks.text: You have now spent six full modules getting fluent with individual tools: creating and reshaping NumPy arrays, building and filtering pandas DataFrames, merging and grouping data, cleaning messy columns and engineering new ones, working with time series, and making all of it run fast on real sized data. Every one of those skills got taught mostly in isolation, one technique at a time, on its own small example. Real projects do not work that way. A real dataset shows up messy, and it needs several of those techniques applied together, in a specific order, before any model can touch it. That is exactly what this final module is about, and this opening lesson walks through the entire real world workflow end to end, as one coherent pipeline instead of eight separate tricks.

blocks.alt: A four stage flow showing load and inspect, clean and encode, engineer and scale, and split as one continuous pipeline
blocks.caption: The whole preprocessing workflow compressed into four phases. Everything in this lesson fits into one of these boxes.

blocks.text: 1. Welcome to the Final Module

This is NumPy plus Pandas for ML, the seventh and final module of this course, and Data Preprocessing is its opening lesson. Nothing about that placement is an accident. Everything before this module taught you a tool. This module teaches you how to actually use those tools together, on a real dataset, the way you would on the job.

items: NumPy Fundamentals, where you learned arrays, shapes, broadcasting and vectorization
Pandas Fundamentals, where you learned Series, DataFrames, reading data and basic inspection
Data Manipulation, where you learned merging, joining, grouping and reshaping
Data Cleaning and Feature Engineering, where you learned imputation, outlier handling, encoding and scaling
Time Series with Pandas, where you learned datetimes, resampling and rolling windows
Performance Optimization, where you learned to make all of the above run fast on real sized data

blocks.text: Every one of those individual techniques is a piece of a puzzle. This lesson does not add a new piece. It shows you the picture the pieces make once you put them together in the right order, wrap that order into something reusable, and run it start to finish on a small but genuinely messy dataset. Think of everything up to this point as learning individual tools in a shop, and this module as finally building the actual piece of furniture.

Call this "production shaped" as a mental label for the rest of the module. A production shaped workflow is not just correct on one notebook run, it is something you could hand to a teammate, run again next month on fresh data, or wire into a scheduled job, and trust to behave identically every time. That is a different bar than just getting a script to run once, and it is the bar every lesson in this module is aiming at.

blocks.title: What this lesson deliberately skips
blocks.content: You will not get a fresh deep dive into how median imputation works, or the exact formula behind standardization, or the mechanics of one hot encoding. Those lessons already did that job properly, and this lesson names each one as it comes up so you know exactly where to go back if a detail feels fuzzy. What is new here is the order everything happens in, the packaging into one reusable function, and the discipline of applying that function consistently, on train, on test, and later on production data.

blocks.text: 2. The Standard Preprocessing Checklist

Strip away the specifics of any dataset and almost every real preprocessing job follows the same shape. Different teams give the steps slightly different names, some skip a step because their data genuinely does not need it, but the underlying sequence below is close to universal, and it is worth having memorized cold. Picture a typical dataset you would actually work with, say customer signup records used to predict who is about to churn, and every step below maps onto something you would do to that exact dataset before it ever meets a model.
2.1 The Eight Steps In Order
Here is the checklist stated plainly, in the order it typically runs. Hold onto this list, the rest of the lesson keeps coming back to it.

items: Load the raw data, from a CSV, a database, an API, wherever it actually lives
Inspect it, shape, dtypes, missing counts, obvious weirdness, before changing a single value
Handle missing values, decide what a gap in the data should become
Handle outliers, decide what an extreme value should become
Encode categorical columns, turn text categories into numbers a model can actually use
Engineer new features, build columns that carry more signal than the raw ones alone
Scale or standardize numeric columns, put every number on a comparable footing
Split into train and test, the formal boundary between what the model learns from and what it gets judged on

blocks.text: That last step deserves a flag right away. It is listed last because conceptually it is the final boundary you draw before modeling starts, the moment you decide which rows the model is allowed to learn from. In practice though, several of the steps before it, specifically handling missing values, handling outliers, and scaling, involve fitting a statistic, and that statistic is only ever allowed to come from the training rows. The next section untangles exactly what that means.

blocks.alt: Four connected steps: load raw data, inspect the data, handle missing values, handle outliers
blocks.caption: The first half of the checklist: getting the data in and understanding what is actually wrong with it.

blocks.alt: Four connected steps: encode categories, engineer features, scale numeric columns, split train and test
blocks.caption: The second half of the checklist: shaping the data into something a model can consume.

blocks.text: 2.2 Why This Order Matters

Cleaning and encoding come before scaling for a very concrete reason. A scaler works by computing something like a min, a max, a mean, or a standard deviation on a column of numbers. Hand it a column that still contains text categories and it either throws an error or, worse, silently does something meaningless. So the column has to already be numeric, meaning missing values filled and categories encoded, before a scaler ever touches it. Outliers matter for the exact same reason you already met in the data normalization lesson: a single extreme value can crush every normal value in a column into a tiny sliver near zero, so outliers get capped or removed before scaling, never after.

blocks.alt: A raw column with text and an outlier taking two paths: scaling first breaks on the text, while cleaning and encoding first lets scaling work correctly
blocks.caption: Scale a column before it is clean and encoded, and the scaler either crashes or lies to you.

blocks.text: Now for the split. The reason it has to happen before you fit any statistic, even though it is listed last on the checklist above, comes straight from the data leakage concept you already met in both the missing value imputation lesson and the data normalization lesson. Fitting a median, a percentile cap, or a mean and standard deviation on rows that include your test set means information about those supposedly unseen rows quietly leaks into a number your training process depends on. The model then looks better during evaluation than it will ever perform on genuinely new data. In real pipelines, this usually means splitting the raw dataset early, right after the inspection step, and then running the missing value, outlier, encoding, and scaling steps on the training and test partitions separately, always fitting on train and only ever transforming the test side.

blocks.alt: Two paths from a dataset: fitting a scaler on the full dataset leaks test statistics into training, while splitting first and fitting only on train keeps the transformation honest
blocks.caption: Same dataset, same scaler, two different outcomes depending entirely on when you split.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Doing This Out of Order","What Goes Wrong"],"rows":[["Scaling before encoding","The scaler tries to compute a mean or a min and max on text values and either errors out or produces numbers that mean nothing"],["Scaling before handling outliers","One extreme value dominates the min, max, mean, or standard deviation, crushing every normal value into a narrow sliver near zero or one"],["Fitting a scaler or imputer before splitting","Statistics from the test set leak into training, so the model looks better during evaluation than it will ever perform in production"],["Engineering features after scaling","Newly created columns land on a completely different scale than everything else, so anything you engineer that needs scaling has to exist before the scaling step runs"]]}

blocks.title: Order is not a style preference here
blocks.content: Every row in the table above is a real, common bug, not a theoretical edge case. The checklist order exists because each step depends on a guarantee the previous step provides: numeric columns exist before you scale them, outliers are handled before they distort a statistic, and the training partition never sees test rows before something gets fit on it. Skipping the order does not usually crash your code. It just quietly produces a worse, or a dishonestly optimistic, model.

blocks.text: 4. From a One Off Script to a Reusable Function

Knowing the checklist is one thing. Applying it consistently, every single time, on every dataset that touches your model, is a different problem entirely, and it is where most of the real damage in production ML actually happens.
4.1 The Problem With Ad Hoc Preprocessing

Picture the common way this actually gets built the first time. You open a notebook, load the data, and write eight cells, one per checklist step, each one mutating the DataFrame a little more until it is model ready. It works. The model trains. Three weeks later a fresh batch of data arrives and needs the exact same treatment, so you scroll up, copy the eight cells into a new notebook, and run them again, maybe fixing a column name along the way. This is an ad hoc script, and it is a completely normal way to first solve the problem.

blocks.alt: A new notebook cell with copy pasted steps that quietly drift over time, contrasted with a reusable function that runs the same steps on every call
blocks.caption: Copy pasted preprocessing feels fine right up until it silently stops matching itself.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Aspect","Ad Hoc Script","Reusable Function"],"rows":[["How each step gets applied to new data","Retyped or copy pasted by hand, hoping you remember every line","Called by name, guaranteed to run every step in the same order"],["A fitted statistic like a median or an encoder category list","Easy to forget to reuse, easy to accidentally refit on the wrong data","Stored once and passed back in explicitly on every later call"],["What happens when the raw schema shifts slightly","Breaks silently somewhere in the middle of a long notebook","Fails fast at one obvious point you can actually debug"],["How training and production preprocessing relate","Two separate pieces of code that quietly drift apart over time","The exact same function, called in both places"]]}

blocks.text: A table comparing them side by side makes the pattern obvious: every single row favors the function, not because ad hoc scripts are badly written, but because nothing about a script structurally prevents the two copies from drifting apart, while a function makes drifting apart nearly impossible.
4.2 Training and Production Quietly Drifting Apart

Here is the specific, real failure mode ad hoc scripts cause. The notebook that trained your model fills missing age with the training median, caps income at the 99th percentile, and one hot encodes three cities. Months later, someone writes a separate script for the production service that also fills missing age, but uses a slightly different median because it was computed on a different slice of data, or forgets the income cap entirely, or encodes the cities in a different column order. Nothing crashes. The service runs, returns predictions, and every one of those predictions is now quietly wrong, because the data the model sees at prediction time was not prepared the same way as the data it learned from.

blocks.alt: Training notebook preprocessing on one path leading to a trained model, while a separate production script with slightly different preprocessing steps leads to a silent prediction bug
blocks.caption: Two codebases doing almost the same thing is worse than one codebase doing it consistently.

blocks.title: Drift like this is one of the most common real ML bugs
blocks.content: It almost never announces itself. There is no error message, no failed test, no red flag in a dashboard. The model simply performs worse in production than it did in evaluation, and by the time anyone notices, the two preprocessing paths have usually drifted further apart. The fix is not more discipline or more careful copy pasting. The fix is making it structurally impossible to have two versions in the first place, which is exactly what wrapping the checklist into a single function buys you.

blocks.text: 4.3 Wrapping the Checklist Into One Function

The fix is simpler than it sounds: write one function that takes a raw DataFrame in and returns a model ready DataFrame out, with every checklist step happening inside it, in the fixed order from section 2. Call that exact same function on your training data, your test data, and later on every new row that shows up in production. Same code, same order, every time, by construction rather than by memory.

code.content:
def preprocess(df, fitted_stats=None):
    df = df.copy()
    # ... every checklist step happens in here, in order ...
    return df, fitted_stats

blocks.text: The second argument is the part that makes this leakage safe rather than just tidy. On the first call, on your training data, you pass nothing in, and the function learns whatever statistics it needs, a median here, a cap there, a mean and standard deviation for scaling, and hands them back to you alongside the cleaned DataFrame. On every later call, on test data or on a brand new production row, you pass those exact same learned statistics back in, and the function reuses them instead of learning anything fresh. That returned dictionary is, in miniature, exactly what a real fitted transformer object is: a set of numbers learned once, from training data only, and replayed identically everywhere else.
5. Looking Ahead: The Scikit-Learn Pipeline

The hand rolled fitted_stats dictionary from the previous section is a perfectly reasonable way to learn the pattern, but real projects almost always reach for a more formal tool once things get serious: scikit-learn's Pipeline class. A Pipeline chains together the exact kind of steps you just built by hand, imputers, encoders, scalers, and gives the whole chain a single fit and a single transform, formalizing the fit on train, transform everywhere pattern you already know from SimpleImputer and StandardScaler in earlier lessons.

blocks.alt: Raw training data going into a pipeline fit on train, producing one pipeline object that then transforms both test data and production data identically
blocks.caption: A Pipeline is the formal, production grade version of the fitted_stats dictionary from the last section.

code.content:
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

pipeline = Pipeline([
    ('impute', SimpleImputer(strategy='median')),
    ('scale', StandardScaler()),
])

pipeline.fit(X_train)                        # learns statistics from train only
X_test_ready = pipeline.transform(X_test)     # reuses those exact statistics

blocks.text: A Pipeline object can also be saved to disk as a single artifact, sits neatly inside cross validation and hyperparameter search, and handles a detail that a hand rolled function like the one in this lesson can get wrong, keeping encoded columns consistent even when a category is missing from one split but present in another. That last point matters enough that the worked example ahead calls it out directly.

Real datasets usually mix numeric columns that need scaling with categorical columns that need encoding, often in the same DataFrame. A companion tool called ColumnTransformer handles exactly that split, routing each column to the right step inside a single Pipeline, so age gets scaled while city gets encoded, all inside one object with one fit and one transform. That combination, Pipeline plus ColumnTransformer, is close to the industry default for this entire checklist once a project moves past the exploration stage.

blocks.title: Not covered in depth here
blocks.content: The full mechanics of Pipeline, ColumnTransformer, and how to mix them with custom transformers get their own proper treatment later in the Preparing Data for Scikit-Learn lesson in this same module. For now, just recognize the shape: fit once on train, transform everywhere, exactly the pattern this whole lesson has been building toward by hand.

blocks.text: 6. Worked Example: One Complete Preprocessing Function

Time to put the whole checklist together on one small, deliberately messy dataset: eight customer signup records, used to predict churn, with missing ages, one dramatic income outlier, inconsistently cased city names, and a raw date column that needs turning into something a model can use.
6.1 The Raw Messy Data
Here is the dataset exactly as it might arrive from a real signup database, problems and all.

items: Two rows have a missing age, plain NaN values
One row has an income of 640000 against a normal range of roughly 47000 to 62000, a clear outlier
The city column mixes casing and stray whitespace: New York, new york, and NEW YORK are all the same city
signup_date is stored as plain text, not a real datetime, so nothing about how long ago someone signed up is usable yet
churned is the target column and should never get scaled or encoded like the rest

blocks.text: Running raw.info() and raw.isna().sum() on this DataFrame, straight from the Data Inspection lesson, would immediately surface the two missing ages and confirm every other column has a value in every row. That is exactly the point of inspecting before touching anything: it tells you precisely which of the remaining checklist steps this particular dataset actually needs, rather than guessing.

blocks.alt: A raw customer DataFrame with four labeled problems: missing age values, an extreme income outlier, city stored as text, and inconsistent casing
blocks.caption: Four ordinary, extremely common problems, all sitting in one eight row dataset.

blocks.text: 6.2 Building the Function Step by Step

Notice that step 1, loading the data, already happened above, before this function is ever called, since the function takes an already loaded DataFrame as its input. Step 8, splitting, happens outside the function too, and deliberately right before you call it, so the function itself only ever sees rows it is allowed to learn from. Everything from step 2 through step 7 lives inside the function body, each one labeled with a comment matching the checklist numbering from section 2.

code.content:
def preprocess(df, fitted_stats=None):
    df = df.copy()  # never mutate the raw input; step 1 already happened before this call

    # Step 2: inspect, a lightweight guard rail rather than a full exploration
    required = {'age', 'income', 'city', 'signup_date', 'churned'}
    assert required.issubset(df.columns), 'raw schema does not match what this function expects'

    if fitted_stats is None:
        fitted_stats = {}

    # Step 3: handle missing values, median age learned once and reused
    if 'age_median' not in fitted_stats:
        fitted_stats['age_median'] = df['age'].median()
    df['age'] = df['age'].fillna(fitted_stats['age_median'])

    # Step 4: handle outliers, cap income at a fitted 99th percentile
    if 'income_cap' not in fitted_stats:
        fitted_stats['income_cap'] = df['income'].quantile(0.99)
    df['income'] = df['income'].clip(upper=fitted_stats['income_cap'])

    # Step 5: encode categorical columns, clean the text, then one hot encode
    df['city'] = df['city'].str.strip().str.lower()
    df = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=['city'], drop_first=True)

    # Step 6: engineer a new feature from the raw signup date
    df['signup_date'] = pd.to_datetime(df['signup_date'])
    reference_date = pd.Timestamp('2024-06-01')
    df['days_since_signup'] = (reference_date - df['signup_date']).dt.days
    df = df.drop(columns=['signup_date'])

    # Step 7: scale numeric columns using statistics fitted on train only
    numeric_cols = ['age', 'income', 'days_since_signup']
    for col in numeric_cols:
        if f'{col}_mean' not in fitted_stats:
            fitted_stats[f'{col}_mean'] = df[col].mean()
            fitted_stats[f'{col}_std'] = df[col].std()
        df[col] = (df[col] - fitted_stats[f'{col}_mean']) / fitted_stats[f'{col}_std']

    return df, fitted_stats

blocks.text: A couple of details worth pointing at directly. The numeric_cols list in step 7 deliberately leaves out the one hot encoded city columns, since those already sit at 0 or 1 and scaling them further would not mean anything. And the encoding step above has an honest limitation worth naming out loud: pd.get_dummies only looks at whichever city categories happen to be present in the DataFrame you hand it. If a train and test split ever separated the data such that one side lost a whole category, for example if every "austin" row ended up in training and none in test, the two resulting DataFrames could end up with different dummy columns entirely. This is precisely the kind of subtle mismatch a fitted, reusable encoder, like scikit-learn's OneHotEncoder or the Pipeline mentioned in the previous section, is built to prevent, since it fits a fixed category list once on train and reuses it everywhere afterward.

blocks.alt: The preprocessing function body shown as five labeled stages: inspect guard, handle missing and outliers, encode categories, engineer features, and scale numeric columns
blocks.caption: Every line inside the function maps back to a specific numbered step from the checklist in section 2.

blocks.text: 6.3 Running It End to End

Now step 8, the split, happens first, before preprocess gets called at all. The training call learns every statistic fresh. The test call reuses those exact same statistics and learns nothing new, which is the entire leakage safe pattern from section 2.2 in three lines of code.

code.content:
from sklearn.model_selection import train_test_split

# Step 8: split before any statistic gets fit, this is the leakage boundary
train_raw, test_raw = train_test_split(raw, test_size=0.25, random_state=0)

train_ready, stats = preprocess(train_raw)                 # fits on train, transforms train
test_ready, _ = preprocess(test_raw, fitted_stats=stats)    # reuses the exact same stats, fits nothing new

blocks.text: Notice that the second call throws away the second return value entirely with an underscore, on purpose. The test call is never allowed to update fitted_stats, it only ever reads from it. That single underscore is the whole leakage guarantee, made visible in code.

blocks.text: 6.4 What This Buys You At Prediction Time

This is the entire point of building a function instead of a script. Save stats once, right after training, and reuse it for the rest of the model's life, on every batch of test data and on every single row that shows up in production, without ever refitting anything.

code.content:
import pickle

with open('preprocess_stats.pkl', 'wb') as f:
    pickle.dump(stats, f)

# later, inside the production service
with open('preprocess_stats.pkl', 'rb') as f:
    stats = pickle.load(f)

new_customer = pd.DataFrame([{
    'age': np.nan, 'income': 71000, 'city': ' Chicago',
    'signup_date': '2024-05-20', 'churned': None,
}])
ready_row, _ = preprocess(new_customer, fitted_stats=stats)

blocks.text: That new customer row gets the missing age filled with the same median learned from training months earlier, the same income cap, the same city encoding, and the same scaling, because it is running through the identical function with the identical stats. No separate production script to keep in sync, no risk of a median that quietly drifted, no risk of a scaler that got refit on the wrong data by accident.

This is also exactly what a fitted scikit-learn Pipeline gives you for free once you move to it, a single object that already bundles its own learned statistics and exposes the same transform call everywhere. The hand rolled stats dictionary in this lesson and a saved Pipeline object are solving the identical problem, one written by hand to make the mechanics obvious, the other written for you and battle tested.

blocks.title: Persist the stats, not just the code
blocks.content: The function definition alone is not enough to reproduce this behavior later, the fitted statistics inside stats are just as essential and need to travel with the model, typically saved alongside it with pickle or joblib. A model file without its matching preprocessing stats is only half of what production actually needs.

blocks.text: 7. Wrap Up and What Is Next

items: The real world preprocessing sequence is close to universal: load, inspect, missing values, outliers, encode, engineer, scale, split
Clean and encode before you scale, since a scaler needs numeric, outlier free columns to work correctly
Split before fitting any statistic, a median, a cap, a mean and standard deviation, or you leak test information into training
Every individual step already has its own dedicated lesson, this one is only about the order and the packaging

Wrap the whole sequence into one function that returns both the cleaned data and the statistics it learned, then reuse that same function and those same statistics everywhere, train, test, and production
scikit-learn Pipeline formalizes exactly this pattern for real projects, and gets its own proper treatment later in this module

blocks.text: From here, the module keeps building on this exact foundation. Feature Selection and Data Transformation come next, followed by Dataset Splitting, which finally gives the formal treatment step 8 has been pointing toward this whole lesson. After that, Statistical Analysis and Correlation Analysis dig into understanding a cleaned dataset more deeply, and the module closes with Preparing Data for Scikit-Learn and Preparing Data for PyTorch or TensorFlow, handing this exact model ready output to the frameworks that actually train on it.

blocks.title: The one habit worth keeping from this lesson
blocks.content: Whenever you find yourself about to fit a statistic of any kind, a mean, a median, a cap, a set of categories, pause and check that you already split the data first, and that the fit only ever touches the training rows. Every other detail in this lesson can be looked up again later. That one habit is the difference between a model that works in production and one that only ever looked good in a notebook.
